title: What the November deliberations add to Norges Bank’s 4.5% decision
summary: Norges Bank’s Monetary Policy and Financial Stability Committee unanimously held the policy rate at 4.5% on 4 November. The meeting page released the next day includes the members’ assessment of new information since September, alongside the decision, press conference and statement. Its starting point was the forecast published on 24 September. That forecast had the rate staying near 4.5% for a time and then easing somewhat, inflation approaching 2% in 2029 and registered unemployment edging up. The November meeting produced no new forecast. The question before members was whether the intervening news justified a departure from that assessment (deliberations, opening and monetary policy assessment).

Domestic inflation and imported goods told different stories. Consumer prices rose 3.4% in the year to September and the index excluding energy and adjusting for tax changes rose 3.0%. The average of underlying indicators was close to that second figure and little changed from August. Domestically produced goods and services were more expensive than the September projection implied, while imported consumer goods inflation was lower than expected. The Bank’s combination of short-term forecasting models, SMART, continued to give a near-term outlook close to the previous projection. Members considered the past rise in business costs relevant to how long domestic inflation might stay high. The inflation chart in the Governor’s slides plots both national measures against the target and shows why a single month near the forecast provided limited grounds for changing course (deliberations, inflation; presentation, slide 3).

The external news contained offsetting price signals. Spot oil had fallen since September, while oil futures had risen somewhat and both spot and futures prices for gas and electricity had increased. Other commodity prices, including aluminium and several agricultural products, had fallen. Imported goods faced rising external price impulses as expected, while an appreciation of the krone against several currencies made imports cheaper in domestic currency, other things equal. Trading-partner activity in the third quarter appeared somewhat stronger than projected. Market expectations for Norwegian rates had edged down since the September report, although prices still implied a rise by the end of the first half of 2027. This was a description of market pricing, distinct from the Committee’s conditional assessment (deliberations, international economy and financial markets).

Capacity utilisation was judged slightly below normal in September. Since then, payroll figures had suggested a little more employment growth than expected. Registered unemployment remained 2.0% in October and survey unemployment had changed little. Slide 4 plots the survey and register measures separately. Household card spending and wholesale and retail sales pointed to broadly expected consumption growth. Seasonally adjusted house prices also tracked expectations, while new home sales and building permits remained very low. Members saw little evidence of a substantial change in the demand outlook. The proposed 2027 fiscal budget was assessed as having a broadly neutral effect on next year’s activity (deliberations, activity and labour market).

The Committee continued to see a risk that a long period of above-target inflation would make the process of bringing it down harder. Members also wanted to avoid imposing more restraint on an economy already operating below normal capacity than was necessary. They retained the option of a further increase depending on the inflation outlook. The deliberations do not identify individual members’ views or count how many expressed each observation. The next full set of projections was scheduled for 17 December, giving readers a specific point at which to compare a revised forecast with September’s baseline (deliberations, monetary policy assessment and note 1).

questions.question: Which domestic prices accounted for the surprise against September’s forecast?
questions.detail: Compare the Bank’s archived September forecast vintage with detailed consumer-price releases and subsequent releases for domestically produced goods and services. Trace contributions and persistence separately, then compare them with wage and other business-cost measures. This would show whether a small group of volatile prices or a broader group of suppliers continued to charge more than projected.

questions.question: How quickly did the stronger krone offset external cost increases?
questions.detail: Match import-price series by product and invoicing currency with dated exchange rates, energy prices and retail prices. Compare goods whose input prices rose with goods less exposed to energy costs. Allow for a delay between orders and retail repricing. The exercise could explain why external price impulses rose even as measured imported consumer goods inflation undershot the forecast.

questions.question: Which evidence would most change the assessment of spare capacity?
questions.detail: Compare first releases and revisions to employment, registered unemployment and the Labour Force Survey with the September projection and the Bank’s next forecast. Add new home sales, permits and household spending to see whether soft construction activity spread to wider demand. Record the vintage available at each meeting so subsequent revisions cannot influence the reconstruction of members’ November information set.
